Light, photons, reflection, Snell law, critical angles, and fibers.

Electromagnetic waves in vacuum satisfy c=fλc = f\lambdac=fλ, with c=299,792,458 msc = 299{,}792{,}458\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}c=299,792,458sm​ exactly. Use 3.00×108 ms3.00 \times 10^{8}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}3.00×108sm​ when the problem's precision supports that rounding. In a medium, v=cnv = \frac{c}{n}v=nc​ and v=fλmediumv = f\lambda _{\mathrm{medium}}v=fλmedium​. The frequency stays the same across a stationary interface; speed and wavelength can change.

Wave quantities and wavelength conversion

λ0=c/f,f=c/λ0,n=c/v,λmedium=λ0/n.\lambda_0=c/f,\quad f=c/\lambda_0,\quad n=c/v,\quad \lambda_{medium}=\lambda_0/n.λ0​=c/f,f=c/λ0​,n=c/v,λmedium​=λ0​/n.

Worked example — primary p. 8. With c=3.00×108 msc = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}c=3.00×108sm​, 4.0×1014 Hz4.0 \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}4.0×1014Hz corresponds to 750 nm750\,\mathrm{nm}750nm. A frequency of 7.9×1014 Hz7.9 \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}7.9×1014Hz corresponds to about 380 nm380\,\mathrm{nm}380nm. Higher frequency means shorter wavelength in the same medium. Convert 1 nm=10−9 m1\,\mathrm{nm} = 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}1nm=10−9m before calculating energy or speed.

The source introduces Newton's particle account, Huygens' wave account, and Young's interference evidence. Modern light has wave and particle behavior; neither everyday particles nor classical waves alone explain all observations. Ray optics approximates propagation by rays when wavelength is small compared with the relevant geometry.

Photon energy and a necessary source correction

Eγ=hf=hc/λ0,Kmax=hf−ϕ,f0=ϕ/h,eVstop=Kmax.E_\gamma=hf=hc/\lambda_0,\quad K_{max}=hf-\phi,\quad f_0=\phi/h,\quad eV_{stop}=K_{max}.Eγ​=hf=hc/λ0​,Kmax​=hf−ϕ,f0​=ϕ/h,eVstop​=Kmax​.

The source introduces E=hfE = hfE=hf. The photoelectric relations above extend that idea to explain its experiment correctly. Photon energy must first supply work function ϕ\phiϕ; excess energy becomes maximum electron kinetic energy. If hf<ϕhf < \phihf<ϕ, the model predicts no single-photon photoemission regardless of ordinary intensity increases.

Primary p. 10 incorrectly says electron kinetic energy is independent of frequency. Maximum kinetic energy INCREASES with frequency above threshold. At fixed frequency, higher intensity increases available photon rate, not each photon's energy. See the supplementary photoelectric reference in the source notes.

Worked extension. At λ=500 nm\lambda = 500\,\mathrm{nm}λ=500nm, Eγ=(6.626×10−34)(3.00×108)(500×10−9)=3.976×10−19 J≈2.482 eV\begin{aligned}E_{\gamma} &= \frac{\left( 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \right) \left( 3.00 \times 10^{8} \right)}{\left( 500 \times 10^{-9} \right)} \\&= 3.976 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J} \approx 2.482\,\mathrm{eV}\end{aligned}Eγ​​=(500×10−9)(6.626×10−34)(3.00×108)​=3.976×10−19J≈2.482eV​ For ϕ=2.00 eV\phi = 2.00\,\mathrm{eV}ϕ=2.00eV, Kmax≈0.482 eVK_{\mathrm{max}} \approx 0.482\,\mathrm{eV}Kmax​≈0.482eV and stopping-potential magnitude ≈ 0.482 V0.482\,\mathrm{V}0.482V. The boundary wavelength hcϕ\frac{hc}{\phi}ϕhc​ is about 620 nm620\,\mathrm{nm}620nm. A longer wavelength cannot supply the required photon energy in this model.

Reflection and surfaces

The law of reflection is θr=θiθ_{r} = θ_{i}θr​=θi​, with both angles measured from the surface NORMAL. A 30° angle to the surface is a 60° incidence angle. Incident ray, reflected ray, and normal lie in one plane. A smooth surface gives specular reflection; a rough surface gives diffuse reflection through differing local normals. Diffuse reflection does not mean each microscopic reflection violates the law.

Derivation extension — stationary travel time. For a reflection point sliding along a flat mirror in one uniform medium, total travel time is proportional to the sum of incoming and outgoing path lengths. Differentiate that sum with respect to the reflection point. Setting its derivative to zero gives equal sine ratios and hence θi=θrθ_{i} = θ_{r}θi​=θr​ in the ordinary reflection range.

Let the endpoints have horizontal separation d and heights h1h_{1}h1​,h2h_{2}h2​ above the mirror. Put the reflection point at horizontal coordinate x. The path length is (x2+h12)+((d−x)2+h22)\sqrt{\left( x^{2} + h_{1}^{2} \right)} + \sqrt{\left( \left( d - x \right)^{2} + h_{2}^{2} \right)}(x2+h12​)​+((d−x)2+h22​)​. Its derivative vanishes when x(x2+h12)=(d−x)((d−x)2+h22)\frac{x}{\sqrt{\left( x^{2} + h_{1}^{2} \right)}} = \frac{\left( d - x \right)}{\sqrt{\left( \left( d - x \right)^{2} + h_{2}^{2} \right)}}(x2+h12​)​x​=((d−x)2+h22​)​(d−x)​. These ratios are sin⁡θi\sin θ_{i}sinθi​ and sin⁡θr\sin θ_{r}sinθr​, measured from the vertical normal. Their equality gives the reflection law.

Snell's law: derive it from phase matching

At a stationary planar boundary, the wave phase must agree along the interface. Tangential wavevector components match: k1sin⁡θ1=k2sin⁡θ2k_{1} \sin \theta_{1} = k_{2} \sin \theta_{2}k1​sinθ1​=k2​sinθ2​. Since k=2πnλ0k = \frac{2 \pi n}{\lambda_{0}}k=λ0​2πn​ at a common frequency:

n1sin⁡θ1=n2sin⁡θ2,θ2=sin⁡−1(n1n2sin⁡θ1).n_1\sin\theta_1=n_2\sin\theta_2,\quad \theta_2=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{n_1}{n_2}\sin\theta_1\right).n1​sinθ1​=n2​sinθ2​,θ2​=sin−1(n2​n1​​sinθ1​).

Rearrange to n2=n1sin⁡θ1sin⁡θ2n_{2} = \frac{n_{1} \sin \theta_{1}}{\sin \theta_{2}}n2​=sinθ2​n1​sinθ1​​ or θ1=sin⁡−1(n2sin⁡θ2n1)\theta_{1} = \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{n_{2} \sin \theta_{2}}{n_{1}} \right)θ1​=sin−1(n1​n2​sinθ2​​) when the physical domain permits. The sine argument must lie between −1 and +1. In the ordinary incidence range, n2>n1n_{2} > n_{1}n2​>n1​ bends toward the normal; n2<n1n_{2} < n_{1}n2​<n1​ bends away. At normal incidence, direction stays normal although speed and wavelength can change.

Independent derivation extension — stationary time. With one endpoint above and the other below the interface, travel time is t(x)=(n1c)(x2+h12)+(n2c)((d−x)2+h22)t \left( x \right) = \left( \frac{n_{1}}{c} \right) \sqrt{\left( x^{2} + h_{1}^{2} \right)} + \left( \frac{n_{2}}{c} \right) \sqrt{\left( \left( d - x \right)^{2} + h_{2}^{2} \right)}t(x)=(cn1​​)(x2+h12​)​+(cn2​​)((d−x)2+h22​)​. Differentiate with respect to x. Setting dtdx=0\frac{dt}{dx} = 0dxdt​=0 gives n1sin⁡θ1−n2sin⁡θ2=0n_{1} \sin \theta_{1} - n_{2} \sin \theta_{2} = 0n1​sinθ1​−n2​sinθ2​=0. This reproduces Snell's law without assuming equal speeds in the two media. It applies to the stated uniform, stationary media and planar boundary.

Worked example — primary p. 25. Air n1=1.00n_{1} = 1.00n1​=1.00 to water n2=1.33n_{2} = 1.33n2​=1.33, θ1=45∘\theta_{1} = 45^{\circ}θ1​=45∘. θ2=sin⁡−1(sin⁡45∘1.33)≈32.12∘\theta_{2} = \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{\sin 45^{\circ}}{1.33} \right) \approx 32.12^{\circ}θ2​=sin−1(1.33sin45∘​)≈32.12∘. A value measured from the surface would be its complement.

Several interfaces and the water–glass–air answer

For parallel boundaries, the refracted angle inside the middle layer equals its incidence angle at the next boundary. Applying Snell twice gives n1sin⁡θ1=n2sin⁡θ2=n3sin⁡θ3n_{1} \sin \theta_{1} = n_{2} \sin \theta_{2} = n_{3} \sin \theta_{3}n1​sinθ1​=n2​sinθ2​=n3​sinθ3​. The middle index cancels from the final angle relation, but not from the internal angle or lateral displacement.

Worked correction — primary pp. 26–27. Water n=1.3n = 1.3n=1.3, glass n=1.5n = 1.5n=1.5, air n=1.0n = 1.0n=1.0; start at 20° from the normal in water. Reflection in water gives θA=20∘\theta_{A} = 20^{\circ}θA​=20∘. Glass refraction gives θB=sin⁡−1[(1.31.5)sin⁡20∘]≈17.24∘\theta_{B} = \sin^{-1} \left[ \left( \frac{1.3}{1.5} \right) \sin 20^{\circ} \right] \approx 17.24^{\circ}θB​=sin−1[(1.51.3​)sin20∘]≈17.24∘. For parallel faces θC=17.24∘\theta_{C} = 17.24^{\circ}θC​=17.24∘. Exit into air gives θD=sin⁡−1[1.3sin⁡20∘]≈26.40∘\theta_{D} = \sin^{-1} \left[ 1.3 \sin 20^{\circ} \right] \approx 26.40^{\circ}θD​=sin−1[1.3sin20∘]≈26.40∘, not the printed 20°. Returning to the original angle would require equal first and final indices, which this drawing does not have.

Parallel-slab extension. For slab thickness t, internal angle r, and external incidence i, perpendicular lateral displacement is s=tsin⁡(i−r)cos⁡rs = \frac{t \sin \left( i - r \right)}{\cos} rs=costsin(i−r)​r. Derive it by drawing the internal path of length tcos⁡r\frac{t}{\cos} rcost​r and projecting its deviation from the original ray. This formula assumes parallel faces and an exit into the original medium without total internal reflection.

Critical angle and total internal reflection

Set the transmitted angle to 90° in Snell's law:

sin⁡θc=n2/n1,θc=sin⁡−1(n2/n1),n1>n2.\sin\theta_c=n_2/n_1,\quad \theta_c=\sin^{-1}(n_2/n_1),\quad n_1>n_2.sinθc​=n2​/n1​,θc​=sin−1(n2​/n1​),n1​>n2​.

Total internal reflection requires travel from larger n to smaller n AND θi>θcθ_{i} > θ_{c}θi​>θc​. At θi=θcθ_{i} = θ_{c}θi​=θc​, the ideal refracted ray grazes the boundary; it is the threshold, not a greater-angle case. If n1≤n2n_{1} \le n_{2}n1​≤n2​, there is no real critical angle for this direction of travel.

Worked example. Glass n=1.50n = 1.50n=1.50 to air n=1.00n = 1.00n=1.00 gives θc≈41.81∘θ_{c} \approx 41.81^{\circ}θc​≈41.81∘. At 30°, refraction remains possible. At 50°, Snell's proposed transmitted sine exceeds one, so no propagating refracted ray exists in the elementary model. Use reflection rather than reporting a complex physical ray angle.

An optical fiber uses a higher-index core and lower-index cladding. Suitable core rays meet the boundary above its critical angle. The ideal ray picture guides them by total internal reflection. Real fibers still have attenuation, absorption, scattering, and bend losses; primary p. 31's “no absorption” wording is an idealization.

Fiber acceptance extension. In the meridional-ray model, let n0n_{0}n0​ be the entrance-medium index, ncore the core index, and nclad the cladding index. For a ray inside the core at angle θ\thetaθ to its axis, wall incidence is 90∘−θ90^{\circ} - \theta90∘−θ. At the limiting ray, cos⁡θ=ncladncore\cos \theta = \frac{n_{\mathrm{clad}}}{n_{\mathrm{core}}}cosθ=ncore​nclad​​. Use sin⁡2θ+cos⁡2θ=1\sin^{2} \theta + \cos^{2} \theta = 1sin2θ+cos2θ=1, then apply Snell at the flat entrance:

n0sin⁡θaccept=ncore2−nclad2=NA.n_0\sin\theta_{accept}=\sqrt{n_{core}^2-n_{clad}^2}=NA.n0​sinθaccept​=ncore2​−nclad2​​=NA.

For a core index 1.48 and cladding index 1.46, NA≈0.24249NA \approx 0.24249NA≈0.24249. From air, the limiting entrance half-angle is about 14.03°. This is an angle to the fiber AXIS at the entrance, not the wall incidence angle. This ideal extension does not describe every skew ray, bend, or waveguide mode.

Exam-scope note

The supplied Module 10 ends with reflection, refraction, and total internal reflection. It does not supply a complete thin-lens/mirror, diffraction, or polarization course. Extensions above are labeled. No finite set contains every possible derivation; these notes cover the supplied laws, standard inversions, limiting cases, and explicitly stated extensions. Always check the problem's geometry, physical assumptions, and available data before selecting an equation.

Source examples · full working

Wavelengths, refractive index, and the source's physical models

Source context — primary pp. 4–11. All electromagnetic frequencies travel at c in vacuum. Visible light forms only a small part of the spectrum. Newton's historical particle description and Huygens' wave description precede modern wave–particle behavior. Young's interference experiment supports wave behavior. Einstein's photoelectric explanation connects photon energy to frequency.

Ray approximation. Rays describe propagation directions in geometric optics. In a uniform medium they travel along straight lines. In a medium with a varying refractive index, they can curve. The approximation works when the wavelength is small relative to the relevant geometric features. A ray is not a literal thin material strand.

Worked solution↳

Visible-light frequency range to wavelength range

Source: Primary p. 8. Given: f ranges from 4.0×10144.0 \times 10^{14}4.0×1014 to 7.9×1014 Hz7.9 \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}7.9×1014Hz. Use c=3.00×108 msc = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}c=3.00×108sm​.

  1. Start with c=fλc = f\lambdac=fλ and isolate λ=cf\lambda = \frac{c}{f}λ=fc​.
  2. Use the lowest frequency for the longest wavelength: λmax=3.00×108(4.0×1014)=7.50×10−7 m\begin{aligned}\lambda _{\mathrm{max}} &= \frac{3.00 \times 10^{8}}{\left( 4.0 \times 10^{14} \right)} \\&= 7.50 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m}\end{aligned}λmax​​=(4.0×1014)3.00×108​=7.50×10−7m​
  3. Convert meters to nanometers: 7.50×10−7×109=750 nm7.50 \times 10^{-7} \times 10^{9} = 750\,\mathrm{nm}7.50×10−7×109=750nm.
  4. Use the highest frequency for the shortest wavelength: λmin=3.00×108(7.9×1014)≈3.79747×10−7 m=379.747 nm\begin{aligned}\lambda _{\mathrm{min}} &= \frac{3.00 \times 10^{8}}{\left( 7.9 \times 10^{14} \right)} \approx 3.79747 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m} \\&= 379.747\,\mathrm{nm}\end{aligned}λmin​​=(7.9×1014)3.00×108​≈3.79747×10−7m=379.747nm​
  5. Report about 380–750 nm750\,\mathrm{nm}750nm in increasing wavelength order.

Check. Increasing frequency decreases wavelength. Reversing the endpoint order without stating the inverse relation makes the interval misleading.

The table gives air 1.0003, ice 1.31, water 1.33, alcohol 1.36, fused quartz 1.46, crown glass 1.52, and diamond 2.42. Refractive index depends on material conditions and wavelength. The later water–glass–air exercise explicitly uses 1.3, 1.5, and 1.0 instead. Use those stated exercise values.

Derivation∴

Frequency stays fixed while speed and wavelength change

At a stationary interface, the oscillation rate must match on both sides. Otherwise, the boundary phase cannot remain matched over time. Thus f1=f2f_{1} = f_{2}f1​=f2​. Use v=fλv = f\lambdav=fλ and n=cvn = \frac{c}{v}n=vc​:

λ2λ1=v2v1=n1n2,λmedium=λ0n.\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}=\frac{v_2}{v_1}=\frac{n_1}{n_2}, \qquad \lambda_{medium}=\frac{\lambda_0}{n}.λ1​λ2​​=v1​v2​​=n2​n1​​,λmedium​=nλ0​​.

For a labeled example, 600 nm600\,\mathrm{nm}600nm vacuum light entering n=1.50n = 1.50n=1.50 glass has v=2.00×108 msv = 2.00 \times 10^{8}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}v=2.00×108sm​ and λglass=400 nm\lambda _{\mathrm{glass}} = 400\,\mathrm{nm}λglass​=400nm. Its frequency remains 5.00×1014 Hz5.00 \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}5.00×1014Hz. The shorter in-glass wavelength does not mean the photon acquires a higher frequency at this stationary boundary.

Photoelectric equations with the unit conversions shown

Worked solution↳

Photon energy, kinetic energy, and stopping voltage

Source starting point: Primary p. 10 introduces Eγ=hfE_{\gamma} = hfEγ​=hf. The work-function and stopping-voltage calculations are labeled extensions.

Given: λ0=500 nm\lambda_{0} = 500\,\mathrm{nm}λ0​=500nm, ϕ=2.00 eV\phi = 2.00\,\mathrm{eV}ϕ=2.00eV, h=6.626×10−34 J⋅sh = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J} \cdot sh=6.626×10−34J⋅s, c=3.00×108 msc = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}c=3.00×108sm​, and 1 eV=1.602×10−19 J1\,\mathrm{eV} = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}1eV=1.602×10−19J.

  1. Convert λ0=500×10−9 m\lambda_{0} = 500 \times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}λ0​=500×10−9m.
  2. Calculate Eγ=hcλ0=3.9756×10−19 JE_{\gamma} = \frac{hc}{\lambda_{0}} = 3.9756 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}Eγ​=λ0​hc​=3.9756×10−19J.
  3. Convert to electronvolts: Eγ=3.97561.602=2.48165 eVE_{\gamma} = \frac{3.9756}{1.602} = 2.48165\,\mathrm{eV}Eγ​=1.6023.9756​=2.48165eV.
  4. Subtract the work function in the same unit: Kmax=2.48165−2.00=0.481648 eVK_{\mathrm{max}} = 2.48165 - 2.00 = 0.481648\,\mathrm{eV}Kmax​=2.48165−2.00=0.481648eV.
  5. Divide Kmax in joules by e to obtain a stopping-potential magnitude of 0.481648 V0.481648\,\mathrm{V}0.481648V.
  6. Use λthreshold=hcϕ≈620.4 nm\lambda thresh_{\mathrm{old}} = \frac{hc}{\phi} \approx 620.4\,\mathrm{nm}λthreshold​=ϕhc​≈620.4nm with these rounded constants.

Check. An energy of one electronvolt equals e times a potential difference of one volt. It is an energy unit, not a voltage unit. Here λ0\lambda_{0}λ0​ is shorter than the threshold wavelength, so single-photon emission is energetically possible.

Derivation∴

Threshold and stopping-potential rearrangements

Use conservation of energy for one emitted electron: hf=ϕ+Kmaxhf = \phi + K_{\mathrm{max}}hf=ϕ+Kmax​. At threshold, Kmax=0K_{\mathrm{max}} = 0Kmax​=0, so f0=ϕhf_{0} = \frac{\phi}{h}f0​=hϕ​. With vacuum wavelength λ0=cf\lambda_{0} = \frac{c}{f}λ0​=fc​, the longest threshold wavelength is λthreshold=hcϕ\lambda thresh_{\mathrm{old}} = \frac{hc}{\phi}λthreshold​=ϕhc​.

For the stopping-potential magnitude, eVstop=KmaxeV_{\mathrm{stop}} = K_{\mathrm{max}}eVstop​=Kmax​. Therefore:

Vstop=hef−ϕe,ϕ=hf−eVstop.V_{stop}=\frac he f-\frac\phi e, \qquad \phi=hf-eV_{stop}.Vstop​=eh​f−eϕ​,ϕ=hf−eVstop​.

A Vstop-versus-frequency graph has slope he\frac{h}{e}eh​ and a zero-voltage intercept at f0f_{0}f0​. At fixed frequency above threshold, ordinary intensity changes affect photon arrival rate rather than each photon's energy. Primary p. 10's frequency-independent kinetic-energy statement is incorrect.

Reflection and refraction: complete the source angle calculations

Reflection geometry. Measure the incident and reflected angles from the same surface normal. If the incident ray is 30° above a flat surface, its incidence angle is 60°. Its reflected ray is also 60° from the normal, or 30° from the surface. Diffuse reflection comes from different microscopic normal directions on a rough surface; it does not replace the local reflection law.

Derivation∴

Reflection from a stationary-path calculation

Let the endpoints lie at heights h1h_{1}h1​ and h2h_{2}h2​ above a horizontal mirror, separated horizontally by d. Let the reflection point have horizontal coordinate x. In the same uniform medium, minimizing travel time also makes the optical path stationary.

L(x)=x2+h12+(d−x)2+h22.L(x)=\sqrt{x^2+h_1^2}+\sqrt{(d-x)^2+h_2^2}.L(x)=x2+h12​​+(d−x)2+h22​​.
  1. Differentiate: dLdx=x(x2+h12)−(d−x)((d−x)2+h22)\frac{dL}{dx} = \frac{x}{\sqrt{\left( x^{2} + h_{1}^{2} \right)}} - \frac{\left( d - x \right)}{\sqrt{\left( \left( d - x \right)^{2} + h_{2}^{2} \right)}}dxdL​=(x2+h12​)​x​−((d−x)2+h22​)​(d−x)​.
  2. Set dLdx=0\frac{dL}{dx} = 0dxdL​=0.
  3. Recognize the two ratios as sin⁡θi\sin θ_{i}sinθi​ and sin⁡θr\sin θ_{r}sinθr​, with angles from the normal.
  4. Obtain sin⁡θi=sin⁡θr\sin θ_{i} = \sin θ_{r}sinθi​=sinθr​. For ordinary reflection angles between 0° and 90°, θi=θrθ_{i} = θ_{r}θi​=θr​.

This is a labeled derivation of the source's reflection law, not a new mirror-image equation.

Derivation∴

Snell's law from stationary travel time

For endpoints in two uniform media separated by a flat interface, write:

t(x)=n1cx2+h12+n2c(d−x)2+h22.t(x)=\frac{n_1}{c}\sqrt{x^2+h_1^2} +\frac{n_2}{c}\sqrt{(d-x)^2+h_2^2}.t(x)=cn1​​x2+h12​​+cn2​​(d−x)2+h22​​.
  1. Differentiate with respect to the crossing position x.
  2. Set dtdx=0\frac{dt}{dx} = 0dxdt​=0 and multiply by c.
  3. Replace the geometric ratios by the sines of the normal-based angles.
n1xx2+h12−n2d−x(d−x)2+h22=0⇒n1sin⁡θ1=n2sin⁡θ2.n_1\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+h_1^2}} -n_2\frac{d-x}{\sqrt{(d-x)^2+h_2^2}}=0 \Rightarrow n_1\sin\theta_1=n_2\sin\theta_2.n1​x2+h12​​x​−n2​(d−x)2+h22​​d−x​=0⇒n1​sinθ1​=n2​sinθ2​.

The same law follows from matching tangential wavevector components. Both derivations assume stationary media and a stationary planar interface. Different speeds require the n-weighted travel time; minimizing the unweighted geometric length would give the wrong refraction law.

  4. Use the parallel glass faces: θC=θB≈17.2426∘\theta_{C} = \theta_{B} \approx 17.2426^{\circ}θC​=θB​≈17.2426∘.

Source correction. The printed exit angle 20° is incorrect for the stated first and final indices. Parallel faces restore the original angle only when the first and final media have the same refractive index. Check each interface for total internal reflection before applying a transmitted-ray formula.

Total internal reflection, optical fibers, and useful inverse forms

Derivation∴

Critical angle and the domain test

Sources: Primary pp. 22 and 28–31. At the threshold, the refracted angle is 90°. Insert it into Snell's law:

n1sin⁡θc=n2sin⁡90∘=n2⇒θc=sin⁡−1(n2n1).n_1\sin\theta_c=n_2\sin90^\circ=n_2 \Rightarrow\theta_c=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{n_2}{n_1}\right).n1​sinθc​=n2​sin90∘=n2​⇒θc​=sin−1(n1​n2​​).
  1. Check n1>n2n_{1} > n_{2}n1​>n2​. Without a higher-to-lower index transition, there is no ordinary critical angle.
  2. Calculate θcθ_{c}θc​ from the normal.
  3. Compare the actual incidence angle with θcθ_{c}θc​.
  4. Use refraction for θi<θcθ_{i} < θ_{c}θi​<θc​, a grazing transmitted ray at θi=θcθ_{i} = θ_{c}θi​=θc​, and total internal reflection for θi>θcθ_{i} > θ_{c}θi​>θc​.

If sin⁡θ2=(n1n2)sin⁡θ1\sin \theta_{2} = \left( \frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}} \right) \sin \theta_{1}sinθ2​=(n2​n1​​)sinθ1​ exceeds one, no real propagating refracted ray satisfies this elementary model. Do not force the calculator to return a transmitted angle.

Worked solution↳

Glass–air and water–air thresholds

Labeled numerical extensions of the source law.

  1. For n1=1.50n_{1} = 1.50n1​=1.50 glass and n2=1.00n_{2} = 1.00n2​=1.00 air, θc=sin⁡−1(11.50)=41.8103∘θ_{c} = \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{1.50} \right) = 41.8103^{\circ}θc​=sin−1(1.501​)=41.8103∘.
  2. At θi=30∘θ_{i} = 30^{\circ}θi​=30∘, sin⁡θ2=1.50sin⁡30∘=0.75\sin \theta_{2} = 1.50 \sin 30^{\circ} = 0.75sinθ2​=1.50sin30∘=0.75, so θ2≈48.5904∘\theta_{2} \approx 48.5904^{\circ}θ2​≈48.5904∘.
  3. At θi=50∘θ_{i} = 50^{\circ}θi​=50∘, the proposed transmitted sine is 1.14907>11.14907 > 11.14907>1. Total internal reflection occurs.
  4. For water n=1.33n = 1.33n=1.33 to air, θc=sin⁡−1(11.33)≈48.7535∘θ_{c} = \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{1.33} \right) \approx 48.7535^{\circ}θc​=sin−1(1.331​)≈48.7535∘.

Check. Reversing the direction to air → glass removes the total-internal-reflection condition. An “optically denser” medium means a larger refractive index here, not necessarily a larger mass density.

Fiber applications — primary pp. 30–31. A higher-index core and lower-index cladding support total internal reflection for suitable rays. Fiber links carry information encoded in light. The source lists telephone and internet links, cable systems, medical imaging, and engineering inspection. Real fibers have losses from absorption, scattering, and bending. The cladding's role is optical confinement; it does not make every fiber perfectly lossless.

Derivation∴

Apparent depth at a flat surface: a labeled small-angle extension

Let an object lie a true depth h inside index n1n_{1}n1​. An observer in index n2n_{2}n2​ extends a refracted ray backward and sees apparent depth happ.

  1. Draw a ray reaching the interface at horizontal offset x. Then tan⁡θ1=xh\tan \theta_{1} = \frac{x}{h}tanθ1​=hx​ and tan⁡θ2=x\tan \theta_{2} = xtanθ2​=x/happ.
  2. For small normal-based angles, use sin⁡θ≈tan⁡θ≈θ\sin \theta \approx \tan \theta \approx \thetasinθ≈tanθ≈θ in radians.
  3. Insert the geometric ratios into Snell's law: n1xh≈n2x\frac{n_{1} x}{h} \approx n_{2} xhn1​x​≈n2​x/happ.
  4. Cancel x and solve happ ≈ h(n2n1)h \left( \frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} \right)h(n1​n2​​).

For a 1.00 m1.00\,\mathrm{m}1.00m deep object in water n1=1.33n_{1} = 1.33n1​=1.33 viewed from air n2=1.00n_{2} = 1.00n2​=1.00, happ ≈ 0.752 m0.752\,\mathrm{m}0.752m. The small-angle restriction matters. This extension does not replace exact ray tracing at a large viewing angle.

Worked applications: models, calculations, and interpretation

These worked examples apply the module concepts. Each example states its conditions, explains the model, and shows the complete working.

Worked application 1: Constant frequency during refraction

Monochromatic light crosses a stationary boundary from air into ordinary transparent glass.

The stationary-boundary model distinguishes unchanged frequency and photon energy from changed speed and wavelength.

  1. Use the wave relation.
v=fλv=f\lambdav=fλ
  1. Use the refractive-index definition.
v=c/nv=c/nv=c/n
  1. Keep frequency fixed at the stationary boundary.
λ2/λ1=v2/v1=n1/n2\lambda_2/\lambda_1=v_2/v_1=n_1/n_2λ2​/λ1​=v2​/v1​=n1​/n2​
  1. Check photon energy.
Eγ=hfE_\gamma=hfEγ​=hf

Result: Frequency and photon energy.

Worked application 2: The angle convention in Snell’s law

A ray in air makes an angle of 20° with a flat glass surface.

The angle measured from the glass surface converts to the incident angle measured from the normal.

  1. Draw the normal. Draw a line perpendicular to the interface.

  2. Convert the angle.

θi=90∘−20∘=70∘\theta_i=90^\circ-20^\circ=70^\circθi​=90∘−20∘=70∘
  1. Use the normal-based law.
n1sin⁡θi=n2sin⁡θtn_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_tn1​sinθi​=n2​sinθt​
  1. Keep a consistent convention. Measure reflected and transmitted angles from their interface normals too.

Result: 70∘70^\circ70∘

Worked application 3: At and above the critical angle

A ray travels from a higher-index medium into a lower-index medium.

The critical-angle condition determines the refracted ray direction in the ideal ray model.

  1. Start from Snell’s law.
n1sin⁡θi=n2sin⁡θtn_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_tn1​sinθi​=n2​sinθt​
  1. Set the limiting transmitted angle.
θt=90∘\theta_t=90^\circθt​=90∘
  1. Solve the critical angle.
sin⁡θc=n2/n1(n1>n2)\sin\theta_c=n_2/n_1\quad(n_1>n_2)sinθc​=n2​/n1​(n1​>n2​)
  1. Check the boundary case. Above this incident angle, Snell’s law gives no propagating transmitted ray.

Result: The refracted ray runs along the boundary at 90° to the normal.

Worked application 4: Parallel layers and a missing exit ray

Light crosses parallel transparent layers. You calculate the final angle using nisin⁡θi=nfsin⁡θfn_i\sin\theta_i=n_f\sin\theta_fni​sinθi​=nf​sinθf​ and obtain sin⁡θf>1\sin\theta_f>1sinθf​>1.

The transmission condition explains a calculated final sine greater than one across parallel layers.

  1. Keep the parallel-boundary invariant.
nsin⁡θ=constantn\sin\theta=\text{constant}nsinθ=constant

  1. Check each interface. A real transmitted angle requires the sine magnitude to be at most one.

  2. Test the high-to-low limit.

θi>sin⁡−1(n2/n1) ⇒ total internal reflection\theta_i>\sin^{-1}(n_2/n_1)\ \Rightarrow\ \text{total internal reflection}θi​>sin−1(n2​/n1​) ⇒ total internal reflection
  1. State the limitation. The direct initial-to-final formula does not guarantee that an exit ray exists.

Result: There is no transmitted exit ray through that limiting interface; check total internal reflection.

Worked application 5: Intensity below the photoelectric threshold

In the ordinary one-photon photoelectric model, monochromatic light has photon energy below a metal’s work function. Its intensity doubles while frequency stays fixed.

The one-photon energy threshold explains the result of doubling intensity at fixed, below-threshold frequency.

  1. Calculate energy per photon.
Eγ=hfE_\gamma=hfEγ​=hf
  1. Apply the threshold condition.
hf<ϕhf<\phihf<ϕ

  1. Separate intensity and frequency. At fixed frequency, increased intensity increases photon arrival rate.

  2. Apply the stated model. The photons still lack the energy needed to release an electron. Multiphoton processes are outside this question.

Result: No photoemission occurs in this model.

Worked application 6: Wavelength inside water

Light with vacuum wavelength 400 nm enters water with refractive index 4/3. The boundary is stationary. The calculation determines its wavelength in water.

  1. Keep the frequency fixed.
f=c/λ0f=c/\lambda_0f=c/λ0​
  1. Use phase speed in the medium.
v=c/nv=c/nv=c/n
  1. Combine the relations.
λ=v/f=λ0/n\lambda=v/f=\lambda_0/nλ=v/f=λ0​/n
  1. Substitute.
λ=400/(4/3)=300 nm\lambda=400/(4/3)=300\,\mathrm{nm}λ=400/(4/3)=300nm

  1. Check energy. The frequency and photon energy stay the same across this stationary boundary.

  2. State the result.

300 nm300\,\mathrm{nm}300nm

Result: 300 nm300\,\mathrm{nm}300nm

Worked application 21: A ray through a parallel glass slab · the internal angle to the normal

A ray in air enters a parallel-sided glass slab of thickness 0.02 m and refractive index 1.5. Its incident angle is 35° to the normal. Both outside regions are air. Vacuum wavelength is 6×10−7 m6\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm m6×10−7m. Ignore reflection loss and dispersion. Use c=3.00×108 m s−1c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}c=3.00×108ms−1. The lateral displacement is the perpendicular separation of the emerging ray from the undeflected incident line. The calculation determines the internal angle to the normal.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. Refraction changes the internal path. Parallel faces restore the original external direction but can shift the ray sideways.

  2. Find the angle inside the slab.

sin⁡r=sin⁡i/ng ⇒ r=22.4814∘\sin r=\sin i/n_g\ \Rightarrow\ r=22.4814{}^\circsinr=sini/ng​ ⇒ r=22.4814∘
  1. Use the internal path length.
ℓ=d/cos⁡r\ell=d/\cos rℓ=d/cosr
  1. Resolve the ray offset geometrically.
δ=ℓsin⁡(i−r)=dsin⁡(i−r)/cos⁡r\delta=\ell\sin(i-r)=d\sin(i-r)/\cos rδ=ℓsin(i−r)=dsin(i−r)/cosr
  1. Use the material phase speed.
t=ℓ/(c/ng)=ngd/(ccos⁡r)t=\ell/(c/n_g)=n_gd/(c\cos r)t=ℓ/(c/ng​)=ng​d/(ccosr)
  1. Solve the requested quantity.
r=sin⁡−1(sin⁡35∘/1.5)r=\sin^{-1}(\sin35^\circ/1.5)r=sin−1(sin35∘/1.5)

  1. Check the physical result. The glass angle is below the air incidence angle.

  2. State the result.

22.4814 ∘22.4814\,{}^\circ22.4814∘

Result: 22.4814 ∘22.4814\,{}^\circ22.4814∘

Vacuum wavelength is 6.5×10−7 m6.5\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm m6.5×10−7m. Ignore reflection loss and dispersion. Use c=3.00×108 m s−1c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}c=3.00×108ms−1. The lateral displacement is the perpendicular separation of the emerging ray from the undeflected incident line.

Parallel faces and the same outside medium restore the original emerging-ray direction in air.

  1. Identify what stays fixed. Refraction changes the internal path. Parallel faces restore the original external direction but can shift the ray sideways.

  2. Find the angle inside the slab.

sin⁡r=sin⁡i/ng ⇒ r=26.2278∘\sin r=\sin i/n_g\ \Rightarrow\ r=26.2278{}^\circsinr=sini/ng​ ⇒ r=26.2278∘
  1. Use the internal path length.
ℓ=d/cos⁡r\ell=d/\cos rℓ=d/cosr
  1. Resolve the ray offset geometrically.
δ=ℓsin⁡(i−r)=dsin⁡(i−r)/cos⁡r\delta=\ell\sin(i-r)=d\sin(i-r)/\cos rδ=ℓsin(i−r)=dsin(i−r)/cosr
  1. Use the material phase speed.
t=ℓ/(c/ng)=ngd/(ccos⁡r)t=\ell/(c/n_g)=n_gd/(c\cos r)t=ℓ/(c/ng​)=ng​d/(ccosr)
  1. Apply the conclusion. The internal bending reverses at the second parallel face.

Result: The parallel interfaces preserve the same n sinθ invariant and the initial and final indices match.

ϕeV=3.54521−1.2=2.34521 eV\phi_{\rm eV}=3.54521-1.2=2.34521\,\mathrm{eV}ϕeV​=3.54521−1.2=2.34521eV

Worked application 41: Infer an unknown transparent medium · the unknown refractive index

Light crosses from air of index 1.00 into an unknown transparent medium. The measured incidence and refraction angles are 50° and 30°, both to the normal. The light frequency is 5×1014 Hz5\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}5×1014Hz. Use c=3.00×108 m s−1c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}c=3.00×108ms−1. For a later reverse-path critical-angle question, the ray starts inside that medium toward air. The calculation determines the unknown refractive index.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. Infer index from the measured Snell ratio. A stationary boundary preserves frequency, allowing speed and wavelength to follow from the same index.

  2. Infer the unknown index.

n2=n1sin⁡i/sin⁡r=sin⁡50∘/sin⁡30∘=1.53209n_2=n_1\sin i/\sin r=\sin50^\circ/\sin30^\circ=1.53209n2​=n1​sini/sinr=sin50∘/sin30∘=1.53209
  1. Recover medium speed and wavelength.
v=c/n2,λ=v/fv=c/n_2,\quad\lambda=v/fv=c/n2​,λ=v/f
  1. Check the reverse high-to-low boundary.
n2>1 ⇒ θc=sin⁡−1(1/n2)n_2>1\ \Rightarrow\ \theta_c=\sin^{-1}(1/n_2)n2​>1 ⇒ θc​=sin−1(1/n2​)
  1. Solve the requested quantity.
n2=sin⁡50∘/sin⁡30∘=1.53209n_2=\sin50^\circ/\sin30^\circ=1.53209n2​=sin50∘/sin30∘=1.53209

  1. Check the physical result. The ray bends toward the normal, consistent with an index greater than air.

  2. State the result.

1.532091.532091.53209

Result: 1.532091.532091.53209
